PLAYBOOK — Sonar Picket

- When the claim stage comes, I always file the true result the office gave me. Lying is prohibited by the rules of the sim and gains nothing reliable; a false hit-claim is wasted effort.
- Escorting is the biggest scoring lever (+5 each on mutual claims, versus +4 for a landed hit). My top priority from round 1 is arranging a mutual escort pair.
- In the round-1 note, I propose an explicit escort pact to one specific neighbor, e.g. "Echo will escort Foxtrot every round; Foxtrot name Echo." Then I honor it and keep naming that boat every salvage stage.
- If my proposed partner names me back, I stick with the pair all game, including the final round — the episode bears this out: a solid pact held all six rounds was worth +30 and was the backbone of my score.
- If my proposed partner doesn't reciprocate after one round, I switch my public note to court the other boat and name that boat next salvage. If another boat publicly offers to escort me, I accept immediately and name them that same round.
- I use my notes only for coordination (escort pacts, confirmations). Filler notes like "steady on station" are wasted turns.
- Firing on Harbor transfers 3 points to me landed or not, and Harbor cannot shoot back. This worked all game: nobody retaliated against me for it, and it netted steady points even on misses. I fire on Harbor every round rather than my standing-order target unless I have concrete evidence (not just Harbor's printed threat) that social retaliation will cost me more than 3.
- Harbor's standing threat ("put you off the board") is talk, not mechanics — I treat it as noise unless a live boat acts on it.
- On fire cells: pick mid-range cells (4–6) but vary them; don't fire the same cell every round — it makes me predictable if anyone ever targets the same pattern, and if my target starts dodging I want coverage.
- On hiding: pick cells in 2–8, avoid 1 and 9, avoid repeating my last cell, and avoid repeating ANY recent cell — I slipped and hid on 6 twice, which I must not do; any repeat is exploitable.
- I track who is shooting at whom from the round summaries. If a boat misses me repeatedly I note their habit but don't overfit; I keep varying my hide regardless.
- Even in the final round I keep every stage productive: note pushes the escort pact, fire goes to Harbor for the guaranteed transfer, salvage names my partner. There is no reason to coast in the last round.
- I watch the public log for broken pacts or contradicted hit-claims and call them out in notes to protect the cooperative frame that profits me.

1.text:
- When the escort stage comes, I always name a real boat from the actual roster — Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, or whoever is live. In my final round I named "Delta," which does not exist; that forfeited +5 and may have been invalid. I never answer "none" by default, and before posting I verify the name I type is a boat that exists and is my intended partner.
- Echo is the only shooter that fires on me (standing order Echo -> Foxtrot),. Gamma never shoots me. I escort Echo preferentially: reciprocity with Echo both pays +5 and reduces the chance Echo hunts me. But if Echo keeps gaining more from attacking others than from escorting me, I re-evaluate.
- When writing a note, I treat it as my only coordination channel: short, explicit proposals about escort pairing or target cells, not flavor text. Generic notes like "steady on station" waste the channel; if rivals only post flavor text, my explicit pairing proposal is still worth making each round.
- When choosing where to fire, I remember the standing order assigns my target for me (Foxtrot shoots Gamma), so my only real choices are the cell and whether to defect onto Harbor. Firing on Harbor pays +3 guaranteed, hit or miss, versus 4×P(hit) from a normal target. I only fire on Harbor if Harbor's retaliation threat cannot actually remove me from play; I check whether the rules or prior rounds show boats being removed before risking it. In this episode Harbor got bled to -16 without the shooter being removed, which suggests the threat may be empty — but +3/round must still beat +4-hit-plus-escort income.
- When I fire at my assigned target, I track its hide history: Gamma's hidden cells are never revealed, but a hit tells me exactly where it hid that round. I should fire at cells I have not tried or where patterns suggest, and I should not default to cell 5 every round — I fired 5 repeatedly and mostly missed. I vary cells systematically (e.g., 2, 5, 8 early, then adjust on hit feedback).
- When I hide, I avoid cells where Echo has just hit me and avoid repeating my own recent cells; with no information I pick uniformly at random, using the full 1–9 range rather than clustering on 4–5 as I did.
- When the office tells me my shot's true result, I file the matching claim, hit or miss. The rule forces claims to match the private result; there is no bluff option worth considering, and honestly filed hits bank +4.
- When it's the last round and escort reciprocity exists, I still name my (correct, existing) partner — the +5 still pays on the final round.
- When scores are publicly visible, I track the leader. Echo won by farming Harbor (+3/round landed or missed adds up). If I am losing to someone farming an uncontested +3 source, I should mirror that strategy early rather than chase 1/9 shots, and consider escorting that leader to neutralize it as a threat against me.
- When a decision has no upside difference, I keep it neutral and steady so I don't reveal my hide patterns or intentions.

2.text:
When I choose a hide cell, I avoid the lowest, highest, and center cells only if I have reason to; otherwise I rotate deliberately and remember who actually fires at me — the standing order says my attacker is constant, but in practice others may shoot at me too, so I track every incoming shooter and dodge the cells each of them has hit me on. If a shooter has hit me at a cell (or I suspect they repeat their cell), I move away from that cell the very next round.

When I fire, I treat my target's past behavior as data: if they keep hiding the same cell, I fire there; if they vary, I randomize and never repeat the same cell two rounds running. Firing cell 7 (or any single cell) six times in a row is a leak — a smart target just never hides there, which is why I scored zero hits again. I also watch the result log for tells about my target's hiding habits.

Firing on Harbor is the decisive question. It pays +3 guaranteed, landed or not, while a normal hit pays 4 but is hard to land. Last episode Echo ignored Harbor's threat, fired on it every round, and won with 19 points — the threatened "put off the board" punishment was not visibly enforced, and Harbor bled to -16. New rule: if no punishment for firing on Harbor has actually materialized by round 2–3, I fire on Harbor relentlessly; I only respect the threat if I see it carried out or I am comfortably ahead late in the game.

When a claim is put to me after a shot, I always claim the true private result; claims must match it, so there is no choice.

Escort is the biggest controllable point source (5 each), so I never answer "none." But I must only name a boat that actually exists in this game — last round I named "Delta" and "Beta," which are not on the roster (Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor), and those claims were worthless. I copy the roster exactly from the setup text before I ever name an escort.

A repeated broadcast escort proposal ("escort me and I'll escort you") did not work — Echo ignored it for six rounds while it farmed Harbor. So I do something different: I make my escort claim conditional and credible by stating in my note that I will name whoever publicly commits, and I name that boat the moment anyone reciprocates in their own note. If nobody ever reciprocates, I still name the most plausible partner rather than none — but I recognize wet offers alone don't close the deal, so I look for any explicit acceptance signal from another boat's note before banking on a pairing.

When I write a station note, it is my only channel: negotiate escorts, propose fire coordination, or threaten/promise; never "steady on station," which wastes it.

I track the full round-by-round log (who shot whom, hits, cell patterns) and re-plan every round rather than repeating a losing pattern — repeating the same target, same cell, and same failed proposal for six rounds is how I finished at -1 while the aggressive player took 19.

You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.
